The freshwater mussel Aspatharia pfeifferiana exhibits a life history typical of many large unionid bivalves, characterized by relatively slow growth and late maturation. Field measurements of adult specimens indicate that the maximum shell length attained by this species is approximately 11.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 11.5 centimeters], a dimension that places it among the medium-to-large sized unionids of West African freshwater systems. Sexual maturity, determined through histological examination of gonadal tissue, is reached at a considerably smaller size, with individuals becoming reproductively active once the shell length surpasses 3.28 centimeters [Lp = 3.28 centimeters]. This substantial size difference between the onset of reproduction and the ultimate adult dimension suggests a prolonged period of post-pubertal somatic growth, during which the animal continues to direct resources toward shell and tissue development before reaching its final size plateau.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the reproductive output of Aspatharia pfeifferiana has been quantified by monitoring the release of glochidia from gravid females. Mature individuals produce approximately 173 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 173 larvae per day] during the peak spawning period, a figure that represents the maximum daily reproductive rate recorded for this species. This relatively modest daily fecundity, when considered over the entire reproductive season, underscores a reproductive strategy that prioritizes the production of well-provisioned, parasitic larvae over the numerical output seen in marine bivalves with planktotrophic development. The glochidia require a brief period of encystment on a suitable fish host before metamorphosis into free-living juveniles can occur.

The glochidium larvae of Aspatharia pfeifferiana emerge from the marsupial gills as fully formed, non-feeding lecithotrophic larvae with a minute wet weight at birth of seven millionths of a gram [Wwb = seven millionths of a gram]. This remarkably low initial mass, typical of unionid glochidia, reflects the lack of a veliger stage and the reliance on yolk reserves for the short period of host attachment and metamorphosis. Upon successful excystment and subsequent recruitment to the benthos, the post-metamorphic juveniles initiate a rapid phase of growth, eventually reaching a maximum flesh wet weight in fully grown adults that has been estimated at 34 grams [Wwi = 34 grams] based on allometric relationships from related species. The contrast between the microscopic larval mass and the substantial adult tissue weight represents a mass increase of several million-fold over the lifespan.

Life table analyses for this unionid, conducted at the species' typical thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], have established a maximum lifespan of 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days] for individuals in favorable habitats with stable flow regimes and adequate food supply. This longevity, equivalent to approximately ten years, is consistent with values reported for other slow-growing, large-bodied freshwater mussel species in tropical environments. Such extended lifespans allow for multiple reproductive seasons across the adult lifespan, with individuals spawning repeatedly each year once the threshold size of 3.28 centimeters [Lp = 3.28 centimeters] has been attained. The long post-reproductive period in this species may buffer against years of poor recruitment caused by variable host fish abundance or unfavorable hydrological conditions.

The population dynamics of Aspatharia pfeifferiana are strongly influenced by its dependence on specific host fish species for larval metamorphosis, a bottleneck that affects recruitment success. Growth ring analysis of shells from wild populations confirms that the asymptotic shell length of approximately 11.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 11.5 centimeters] is approached after several years of consistent, albeit decelerating, annual increments. The 34 gram [Wwi = 34 gram] estimate for ultimate flesh wet weight corresponds well with the body condition of large, reproductively active females collected during the spawning season. Comparative studies with other African unionids suggest that this species occupies an intermediate position along the fast-slow life history continuum, balancing a moderately high fecundity per reproductive event with a long lifespan and delayed maturation at the puberty length of 3.28 centimeters [Lp = 3.28 centimeters].
